title: Nifty slides 1.8% as financials tumble, IT defies the sell‑off
excerpt: The Nifty 50 and Sensex fell close to 1.8% on profit‑taking in financials and a cash‑deficit warning from banks, while the Nifty IT index rose 1.7%. Rising volatility and a weakening rupee set a cautious tone for tomorrow.

What happened

India

The Nifty 50 closed at 25,349.65, down 1.75% from the previous close, while the Sensex slipped to 82,435.99, a 1.77% decline. The Nifty Bank fell sharply to 62,585.35, a 3.17% drop, reflecting stress in the banking sector. In contrast, the Nifty IT managed to climb 1.69% to 31,850.80, buoyed by resilient demand for technology services. Reuters reported that financial stocks led the sell‑off after a four‑week rally, as investors booked gains and reacted to a cash‑deficit signal from banks for the first time since June. The combined effect of profit‑taking and banking concerns outweighed the IT sector’s relative strength, pulling the broad market lower.

Breadth was thin across the NSE. Financials fell 2.31% to 30,017.30, while PSU banks dropped 3.25% to 9,559.65, anchoring the decline. Metals were the worst performer, sliding 3.68% to 11,819.25 as Tata Steel and Hindalco weighed on sentiment. Energy lost 1.78% to 36,655.10 and autos slipped 1.03% to 28,490.70. Pharma and FMCG were marginally down, 0.35% and 0.46% respectively, indicating limited defensive buying. Only the realty index managed a modest gain of 0.31% to 941.85, reflecting isolated buying in property‑related stocks. The overall sector spread underscores a market driven by financial and metal weakness rather than a broad‑based correction.

India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, signalling heightened nervousness after a week of rally‑to‑rally swings. The jump in implied volatility mirrors the sharp pull‑back in financials and the banking cash‑deficit alarm, both of which amplified risk aversion. The index’s movement also tracks the global risk‑off mood sparked by a steep decline in US equities and a modest dip in European markets. Higher VIX levels typically pressure high‑beta stocks, which we saw in the banking and metal indices, while defensive sectors such as pharma and FMCG held up better. The elevated VIX suggests that traders will demand a premium for risk, potentially limiting upside in the next session.

The market’s direction was set by a confluence of domestic and external factors. Profit‑taking after a four‑week rally in financials was the immediate catalyst, as highlighted by Reuters, while Moneycontrol flagged a cash‑deficit warning from banks, adding a layer of fundamental concern. Block‑deal news, including a 22% plunge in APL Apollo Tubes and an 8.5% fall in Tata Steel, reinforced the negative bias in metal and industrial stocks. Meanwhile, a multibagger story in SC Agrotech and a 5% upper‑circuit move in TAKE Limited provided isolated bursts of buying, but they were insufficient to offset the broader sell‑off. The net result was a market that retreated sharply despite pockets of sector‑specific optimism.

Global markets

US equity markets closed sharply lower on Friday, with the S&P 500 down 3.70% to 6,910.39, the Nasdaq tumbling 5.28% to 22,617.73, and the Dow Jones slipping 1.93% to 48,147.33. The sell‑off was driven by a mix of earnings disappointments and concerns over tightening monetary policy, which spilled over into emerging markets. The steep decline in US risk assets heightened global risk aversion, feeding into the Indian market’s volatility and prompting investors to trim exposure to high‑beta sectors such as banking and metals. The US 10‑year Treasury yield fell 2.77% to 4.91%, a move that typically supports equities but was outweighed by the broader market panic.

In Europe, the FTSE 100 managed a modest gain of 0.61% to 10,409.47, indicating some resilience in the UK market despite the turmoil across the Atlantic. Reuters noted that Eurozone growth held steady, though France’s deepening downturn clouded the outlook, while German bond yields edged higher, reflecting a tentative shift back to risk assets. The relative strength in the UK index offered a small counterbalance to the global risk‑off sentiment, but the mixed European data did little to lift Indian equities, which remained under pressure from the dominant US market narrative.

Asian markets presented a mixed picture. The Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% to 56,436.65 on Friday, echoing the US sell‑off, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.12% to 22,383.74 on Monday. Reuters highlighted a bifurcation in China’s steel sector as iron ore demand stayed robust, yet the broader industrial outlook remained cautious. The sharp decline in Japan’s benchmark added to the global risk‑off tone, reinforcing the pressure on Indian exporters and metal stocks. However, the relatively muted move in Hong Kong suggested that regional investors were waiting for clearer cues before committing to riskier assets.

Rupee, rates and commodities

The USD/INR rate closed at 92.91, up 0.27% from the previous close, indicating a weaker rupee against the dollar. A softer rupee raises the cost of imported inputs, particularly crude oil and gold, and can erode corporate margins for import‑dependent firms. The currency move also adds to the pressure on foreign‑exchange‑sensitive stocks, such as those in the IT and pharma sectors, which rely on dollar‑denominated revenues. While a weaker rupee can boost export competitiveness, the prevailing risk‑off sentiment limited any offsetting benefit, leaving the overall market outlook cautious.

US Treasury yields fell to 4.91% on the 10‑year, down 2.77%, while Brent crude slipped 0.78% to $89.25 per barrel. Lower yields typically lower the discount rate for equities, supporting valuations, but the concurrent drop in oil prices eased import‑bill pressures for India, offering a modest tailwind for consumer‑linked stocks. Gold surged 3.00% to $3,620.80, reflecting a flight to safety amid market turbulence. The combination of falling yields, softer oil, and rising gold created a mixed macro backdrop: equity valuations received a modest boost from cheaper financing, yet heightened safe‑haven demand underscored lingering uncertainty.

Bitcoin traded at $61,319.98, up 0.26% from the previous close, marking a small rebound after a sharp sell‑off earlier in the week. While the cryptocurrency market remains in a bearish phase, the modest uptick was noted by Mint as part of a broader, cautious recovery. For Indian investors, crypto exposure is still limited and largely peripheral to the broader equity market dynamics. Nonetheless, the slight rise in Bitcoin highlights that risk‑on assets can find brief support even in a risk‑averse environment, though any spill‑over effect on Indian equities is expected to be minimal.

News that matters

  1. Who is killing Nifty 50 rally? SBI, RIL, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank, Hindalco, JSW among stocks dragging index into red

    Mint

    The Nifty 50 closed at 25349.65 INR, down 1.75%, while the Sensex finished at 82435.99 INR, down 1.77%, as profit-taking erased a four-week rally. Bank Nifty dropped 3.17% to 62585.35 INR, and Nifty IT was the sole gainer at 31850.80 INR, up 1.69%. Financials, PSU Bank, Metal, and Energy were among the worst performers, with the Financials index falling 2.31% and PSU Bank falling 3.25%. Auto declined 1.03% and Pharma edged down 0.35%. The India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70 INR, confirming elevated volatility as traders unwind recent long positions. This matters because the retreat breaks a narrow advance window and exposes the banking system to renewed stress. It affects financials, PSU banks, metals, and auto stocks directly while pressuring broader equity sentiment. The picture would change if institutional flows resume buying or if global cues stabilize after the S&P 500 fell 3.70% and the Nasdaq dropped 5.28% in the closed Friday session. Until then, the trend remains defensive.

  2. Live: Markets snap 2-day rally amid expiry swings; Bank Nifty slips from record high | Closing Bell

    Moneycontrol.com

    Live markets snapped a two-day rally amid expiry swings, with Bank Nifty slipping from record highs. The Nifty 50 fell below 25500 and the Sensex lost roughly 1.5%, dragged down by Tata Steel, Hindalco, Axis Bank, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank. Metal, banking, and finance stocks led the decline, while Nifty IT managed a 1.69% gain. This matters because expiry-driven volatility often amplifies directional moves and can trap leveraged positions, raising the India VIX to 17.70 INR, up 2.18%. It affects the banking and metal sectors most acutely, with spillover risk to the broader Nifty 50. The picture would change if expiry volumes normalize and buying emerges in large-cap defensives. The detail on exact expiry positioning is not yet known, so the extent of algorithmic unwind versus fundamental selling remains unclear.

  3. APL Apollo Tubes shares crash 22%, Tata Steel falls 8.5% as Rs 5,825-crore block deal follows acquisition...

    Moneycontrol.com

    APL Apollo Tubes shares crashed 22% and Tata Steel fell 8.5% following a Rs 5,825-crore block deal tied to an acquisition. The transaction triggered sharp selling in the metal sector, which closed 3.68% lower. This matters because block deals of this size can override daily index flows and force index funds to rebalance, amplifying downside. It directly affects metal stocks and related downstream industries, while also pressuring the Nifty 50 given the sector weight. The picture would change if the buyer disclosed strategic intent or if arbitrage interest absorbs supply. The exact terms of the acquisition beyond the deal size are not yet known, so the sustainability of the sell-off depends on whether more blocks follow.

  4. Financials drag Indian shares down on profit-taking after four-week rally

    Reuters

    Financials dragged Indian shares lower amid profit-taking after a four-week rally, with the Financials index falling 2.31%. Banking cash turned to deficit for the first time since June, adding to liquidity concerns. This matters because financials and PSU banks, down 3.25%, are the backbone of the Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty, so weakness here drags the entire market. It affects banking, finance, and PSU bank stocks, while also influencing the India VIX, which rose to 17.70 INR. The picture would change if foreign institutional investors return to the sector or if domestic cash balances improve. The precise drivers behind the cash deficit beyond the headline timing are not yet known, so the depth of the liquidity squeeze remains uncertain.

  5. India’s banking cash turns to deficit for first time since June

    Moneycontrol.com

    India’s banking cash turned to deficit for the first time since June, signaling a liquidity squeeze at a time when the Nifty Bank fell 3.17% and the Financials index dropped 2.31%. This matters because tighter banking liquidity can constrain credit growth and corporate capex, pressuring earnings expectations across rate-sensitive sectors. It affects banks, PSU banks, and financials, while also weighing on the rupee and bond markets indirectly. The picture would change if the Reserve Bank of India injects liquidity or if deposit inflows resume. The exact magnitude of the deficit and the policy response are not yet known, so the near-term impact on lending rates remains speculative.

  6. Crypto investment amid fall: As Bitcoin hovers near $60K levels, experts answer if investors can expect recovery?

    Mint

    Bitcoin traded below 60000 USD before rebounding to 61319.98 USD, up 0.26%, as crypto markets staged a modest recovery after a sharp sell-off. Experts maintain the broader trend remains bearish. This matters because Indian investors often treat Bitcoin as a risk-on proxy, and its correlation with equities can influence portfolio hedging during volatile sessions like today, when the Nifty 50 fell 1.75%. It affects crypto allocations and high-beta equity sentiment. The picture would change if Bitcoin sustains above 60000 USD with volume confirmation. The specific catalysts for a durable recovery are not yet known, so the rebound may remain fragile.

  7. Up 32% in one month! Small-cap stock under ₹50 hits 5% upper circuit despite weak trends on Dalal Street; do you have?

    Mint

    TAKE Limited, a small-cap stock under 50 INR, hit its 5% upper circuit on 23 November despite weak broader trends, extending a sharp short-term rally. Analysts note improving momentum but warn that low liquidity and repeated circuit movements make the stock risky. This matters because such micro-cap spikes distort index sentiment and can trigger stop-losses in systematic strategies, adding noise to a session where the Nifty 50 fell 1.75%. It affects small-cap indices and retail flow dynamics. The picture would change if institutional participation materializes or if liquidity improves. The exact fundamental rationale for the rise beyond the headline is not yet known, so the sustainability of the move is doubtful.

  8. Multibagger defence stock to buy: Experts see 35% gain on MSCI index rebalancing despite 55% YTD return | Target, SL

    Mint

    A multibagger defence stock has risen from 276 INR to 426 INR in 2026, delivering 55% year-to-date returns, with experts targeting a further 35% gain on MSCI index rebalancing. This matters because index inclusion can force passive inflows, but the stock has already returned 55% this year, leaving limited margin for fresh capital appreciation. It affects the defence and broader Nifty sectors, though its weight is small. The picture would change if the MSCI rebalancing is confirmed or if order books expand. The specific stock identity and exact rebalancing timeline are not yet known, so the magnitude of passive buying remains unquantified.

Our view

bearish Analyst board aligned (3 of 3 views)

The Nifty 50 closed at 25349.65 INR, down 1.75% for the session, while the Sensex fell 1.77% to 82435.99 INR, both recording losses against the previous close. Bank Nifty underperformed sharply, ending at 62585.35 INR, down 3.17%, as profit-taking and a cash deficit in banks dragged the financial system lower. Nifty IT was the sole bright spot, gaining 1.69% to 31850.80 INR, but this could not offset the broad deterioration across the benchmark. The sell-off follows four weeks of gains and aligns with a global risk-off backdrop, where the S&P 500 fell 3.70% and the Nasdaq dropped 5.28% on Friday 20 Nov session, confirming external pressure. The rupee weakened marginally as USD/INR rose 0.27% to 92.91 INR, reflecting capital outflows amid heightened volatility. The house stance remains bearish, with the board aligned on the view that Indian equities face further downside as breadth deteriorates and defensive flows accelerate.

Volatility spiked as the India VIX climbed 2.18% to 17.70 INR, signalling elevated intraday swings and risk aversion heading into expiry. Sector breadth confirms the defensive rotation, with Financials falling 2.31% and PSU Banks declining 3.25%, both hit by profit-taking and emerging liquidity stress. Energy dropped 1.78%, Metal shed 3.68%, and Auto slipped 1.03%, while only Pharma (-0.35%) and Realty (+0.31%) showed relative resilience. The cash deficit in banks, reported for the first time since June, underpins the risk manager's caution and the momentum strategist's conviction that liquidity tightness will constrain risk appetite. Gold jumped 3.00% to 3620.80 USD as a safe-haven bid, and Brent crude eased 0.78% to 89.25 USD, offering limited relief to inflation-sensitive equities. With the FTSE 100 live but trading in isolation, Indian markets remain vulnerable to further foreign selling.

The macro economist notes that the two-day rally in volatility has reversed, with India VIX rising after a brief compression, pointing to expiry-driven swings rather than structural calm. The rupee's 0.27% weakening to 92.91 INR adds currency risk to equity valuations already under pressure from double-digit declines in US and Japanese markets. The Nikkei 225 fell 5.06% on Friday 20 Nov session and the Hang Seng closed 0.12% lower on Monday 23 Nov session, reinforcing that the risk-off tone is global and not confined to domestic factors. US 10Y yields dropped 2.77% to 4.91 USD on Friday 20 Nov session, suggesting a flight to quality that typically hurts growth-sensitive Indian equities. The house view therefore expects the Nifty 50 and Sensex to test lower supports, with Bank Nifty likely to lead further declines as financial conditions tighten.

Tomorrow's session sets up for a cautious open as investors digest expiry-related positioning and the first banking cash deficit since June. The bearish alignment across the strategist, risk manager, and macro economist implies that any rebound will face swift profit-taking, particularly in Financials and PSU Banks. With the S&P 500 closed at 6910.39 USD down 3.70% on Friday 20 Nov session and the Nasdaq at 22617.73 USD down 5.28% on the same session, overseas cues will dominate the opening tone. A break below the recent lows in Bank Nifty could trigger stop-losses across the broader market, while a relief rally in Nifty IT is unlikely to drive breadth. The house expects volatility to remain elevated, with India VIX serving as a real-time gauge of selling intensity through the next expiry cycle.

The board's bearish conviction is supported by deteriorating sector breadth, a weakening rupee, and a global equity sell-off that leaves little room for domestic optimism. Profit-taking after a four-week rally has exposed fragility in bank balance sheets and financial stocks, while the cash deficit report validates the risk manager's caution. With gold rallying and US yields falling, the macro environment favours defensive positioning over equity risk. The house therefore maintains its underweight bias across rate-sensitive and leveraged segments, anticipating that external shocks will continue to override local catalysts in the near term.

Sector calls

SectorCallWhy
FinancialsunderweightFinancials closed 2.31% lower amid profit-taking after a four-week rally and a reported cash deficit in banks, which tightens liquidity and raises credit risk. With the sector leading the broad sell-off and the house stance aligned bearish, we expect continued pressure on earnings multiples and lending growth, warranting an underweight position until balance sheet stress eases.
PSU BankunderweightPSU Banks declined 3.25%, the second-worst performer among tracked sectors, driven by the same banking cash deficit that emerged for the first time since June. This structural liquidity concern, combined with global risk aversion and a weaker rupee, suggests limited near-term recovery in public sector lending metrics, supporting an underweight call.
MetalunderweightMetal fell 3.68%, the deepest decline among NSE sectors, reflecting weak global demand cues and a risk-off tone that penalises commodity-linked equities. With China's steel sector bifurcating and iron ore remaining robust only in select pockets, near-term earnings visibility remains poor, justifying an underweight stance.
EnergyunderweightEnergy dropped 1.78% as Brent crude slipped 0.78% to 89.25 USD, yet the broader risk-off environment and falling global equity benchmarks suggest that even lower input costs cannot offset demand destruction fears. With the house bearish on growth-sensitive segments and external pressure mounting, Energy warrants an underweight rating.
PharmaneutralPharma declined a modest 0.35%, showing the least sensitivity to the banking and financial stress that dominated the session. With defensive characteristics and stable demand, the sector is neither a clear beneficiary nor a victim of the current sell-off, supporting a neutral call pending clearer direction from global risk appetite.
FMCGneutralFMCG fell 0.46%, a relatively contained decline in a session marked by broad equity weakness and a volatile rupee. As a consumption-driven segment with pricing power, it offers limited upside in the current risk-off phase but also avoids the severe damage seen in financials and metals, justifying a neutral stance.
AutoneutralAuto slipped 1.03%, tracking the broader risk-off tone without exhibiting the extreme weakness seen in banks or metals. With input costs moderating and demand remaining mixed, the sector sits at a crossroads, and the house sees no compelling catalyst to tilt the call away from neutral in the immediate session.
RealtyneutralRealty posted a marginal gain of 0.31%, bucking the broad decline and indicating selective buying in rate-sensitive property names. However, with US yields falling and global uncertainty elevated, the sector lacks a strong directional catalyst, so the house maintains a neutral stance until credit conditions and liquidity data clarify the trajectory.

What would change our view

A sharp rebound in the Nifty 50 above the previous close, accompanied by a sustained decline in India VIX below 17.00 INR, would invalidate the bearish thesis by signalling restored risk appetite and an end to expiry-driven volatility.

If the banking cash deficit resolves faster than expected and PSU Banks stage a swift recovery from the 3.25% decline, liquidity stress would fade and the house could be forced to revise Financials and PSU Bank calls toward neutral or overweight.

A decisive break in the USD/INR above 93.50 INR with concurrent foreign inflows into Indian equities would counter the global risk-off narrative, proving that domestic flows can override the S&P 500 and Nasdaq weakness seen in the closed Friday 20 Nov session.

How the analyst board voted
  • Momentum strategist: bearish, conviction 4/5. Broad market weakness: Nifty -1.75%, Sensex -1.77% and Bank Nifty -3.17% with India VIX up 2.18%, signalling heightened volatility and risk aversion. Sector breadth deteriorates: Financials (-2.31%) and PSU Banks (-3.25%) lead the sell‑off amid profit‑taking and a cash deficit in banks, while only IT shows modest gains. Global risk‑off backdrop: US indices plunge (S&P -3.7%, Nasdaq -5.3%), rupee weakens (USD/INR +0.27%), and gold jumps 3%, reinforcing a defensive stance for Indian equities.
  • Risk manager: cautious, conviction 4/5. Broad equity sell‑off with Nifty‑50 and Sensex down ~1.75% and Bank Nifty off 3.17% as profit‑taking hits financials and a cash‑deficit in banks emerges (Reuters, Moneycontrol). India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, signalling heightened intraday volatility amid expiry‑driven swings. USD/INR weakened to 92.91 (+0.27%) while global equity markets posted double‑digit declines, adding currency and external risk pressure.
  • Macro economist: bearish, conviction 4/5. Nifty 50 and Sensex fell ~1.75% while Bank Nifty slumped 3% on profit‑taking and a cash deficit in banks, dragging financials lower. India VIX rose 2.18% to 17.70, indicating heightened volatility after a two‑day rally and expiry‑related swings. The rupee weakened (USD/INR 92.91 up 0.27%) amid a global risk‑off, with US equities down sharply (S&P -3.7%, Nasdaq -5.3%), adding external pressure on Indian equities.

What to watch

  • Whether the Nifty 50 can hold the 25000 INR support level into the next session without fresh foreign selling.
  • The trajectory of India VIX through the next expiry cycle to confirm if volatility expansion is temporary or structural.
  • The rupee's movement against the dollar, specifically if USD/INR breaks above 93.00 INR on sustained dollar demand.
  • Whether Brent crude stabilises below 89.00 USD or resumes its decline, affecting inflation expectations and energy sector margins.
  • If Nifty IT extends its 1.69% gain into a broader rally across defensives, altering the sector leadership pattern.
